content: Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring using cardiotocography (CTG) is a standard practice during labor for women with complicated pregnancies. However, fetal heart rate abnormalities are common and often lead to decisions to expedite delivery, frequently via cesarean section. Fetal scalp stimulation (FSS) is a secondary test used to assess fetal well-being when CTG results are non-reassuring. This method may provide additional reassurance that labor can safely continue. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of FSS as a second-line test for fetal well-being during labor in cases of non-reassuring CTG. Specifically, FSS combined with CTG was compared to CTG alone and to CTG with fetal blood sampling (FBS). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed any form of FSS for evaluating fetal well-being during labor. Quasi-RCTs, cluster-RCTs, and studies published only in abstract form were also eligible, but none were identified. Two trials, involving a total of 377 women, met the inclusion criteria. Both trials were conducted in hospital settings and included women with singleton, term pregnancies (37+0 weeks or more), cephalic presentation, and abnormal CTG findings. Follow-up was conducted until hospital discharge after birth. The first trial, a pilot study conducted in a high-income country (Ireland), involved 50 women and compared CTG combined with digital fetal scalp stimulation (dFSS) to CTG combined with FBS. The second trial, conducted in a lower middle-income country (India), involved 327 women and compared CTG combined with manual fetal stimulation (via abdominal or vaginal scalp stimulation) to CTG alone. Both studies were assessed as having a moderate or unclear risk of bias. While allocation concealment was adequately reported, blinding of participants and healthcare providers was not feasible due to the nature of the interventions. Outcome assessment was either not blinded or unclear. Findings: dFSS and CTG versus FBS and CTG No perinatal deaths were reported, and data on neurodevelopmental disability at 12 months or later were not available. The risk of cesarean section (CS) may be lower with dFSS compared to FBS (risk ratio [RR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 0.92; 1 pilot trial, 50 women). However, the certainty of this evidence is very low, making the findings highly uncertain. No cases of neonatal encephalopathy were reported. The evidence was very uncertain regarding differences between dFSS and FBS for assisted vaginal birth (RR 1.44, 95% CI 0.76 to 2.75) and spontaneous vaginal birth rates (RR 2.33, 95% CI 0.68 to 8.01). Maternal acceptability of the procedures was not reported. Findings: FSS and CTG versus CTG alone Manual fetal stimulation was performed either abdominally (92/164 women) or vaginally (72/164 women). No perinatal deaths were reported, and data on neurodevelopmental disability at 12 months or later were not available. There may be little difference in the risk of CS when comparing manual fetal stimulation combined with CTG to CTG alone (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.18; 1 trial, 327 women). However, the evidence is very uncertain. No cases of neonatal encephalopathy were reported. There may be no differences in the risk of assisted vaginal birth (RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.60) or spontaneous vaginal birth rates (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.21), but the evidence remains very uncertain. Maternal acceptability of abdominal stimulation or FSS was not reported. Thirteen women withdrew consent after randomization due to concerns about fetal well-being. Conclusions: The available evidence is of very low certainty, making it unclear whether fetal scalp stimulation is a safe and effective method for confirming fetal well-being during labor. The evidence was downgraded due to limitations in study design and imprecision. Further high-quality studies with adequate sample sizes are needed to address this research question. Future trials should be conducted in diverse settings, include both preterm and term pregnancies, and standardize the methods of stimulation. An ongoing study (FIRSST) will be incorporated into this review in a future update.
